A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. The main text, figures, table, algorithm and Appendices A–D can be matched reliably; v3 adds Appendix E. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original Monte Carlo simulations, including attention-output distributions, KL divergences and robustness experiments.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B retain the original simulation results in Figures 1–5, including finite-width, low-rank and activation-function experiments.

M1.justification: The attention computation, Tensor Programs construction and Algorithm 1 are unchanged. Appendix E derives an additional property of the existing model.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic attention simulations, including full-rank and low-rank configurations, different sequence lengths, and clipping/ReLU activations. No evaluated dataset or task scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: Figure 2 retains the same comparisons involving Yang's 1/n-scaling regime [Yan19b] and the infinite-head Gaussian limit [HBSDN20]. No comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B retain the same widths, head counts, sequence lengths, initialization and KDE/KL procedures. The 50,000-sample default and 100,000-sample ReLU setting are already present in v2.

E4.justification: The finite-width, scaling, head-count, low-rank, sequence-length and activation analyses are retained unchanged in Figures 1–5 and Appendix B. Appendix E adds a mathematical proof, not an empirical robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 independent trials and one-standard-deviation error bars for the log-KL plots in Figures 1, 3, 4 and 5. No run-count, seed or uncertainty-reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: Figures 1–5 retain identical plot content, including density curves, histograms, log-KL points and error bars. The reported simulation findings concerning convergence, scaling and robustness are unchanged.

T1.justification: New Remark 3.3 and Appendix E establish sub-Gaussian tails by bounding the conditional Gaussian variance. The appendix proves the scalar single-head case and states extensions to multiple heads, vectors and bounded pseudo-Lipschitz score functions. This adds a focused property while retaining the main definitions, assumptions and convergence results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and central finite-head non-Gaussian-limit contribution remain unchanged. The conclusion replaces the conjecture of increasingly heavy-tailed behavior under stacking with a prediction of non-Gaussian limits for both attention and MLP layers.

C2.justification: Section 3 replaces the heavy-tailed characterization with a distinction between non-Gaussian distributions and Gaussian-rate tail decay under bounded score nonlinearities. The conclusion removes speculation about heavy-tail benefits for feature learning. The fixed-sequence-length and batch-size limitation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix B retains the same pseudocode, input-generation instructions, clipping constant C=100, weight initialization and sampling details. Section 5 provides the same simulation-code access information.

R1.justification: The cited works and related-work discussion are unchanged. The paper retains its positioning relative to Gaussian Tensor Programs/NNGP analyses, 1/n scaling and infinite-head approximations.

P1.justification: Localized revisions affect Remark 3.1, the conclusion and acknowledgements, alongside wording and typo edits. Remark 3.3 and Appendix E are added, while the existing narrative organization is largely retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 moves from page 9 to page 10, with associated text reflow. Existing figure and table designs remain unchanged. v3 also introduces stray closing braces in the displayed derivation for Lemma D.8.

improvement.justification: v3 replaces misleading heavy-tail language with an explicit sub-Gaussian tail bound in Appendix E and removes related feature-learning speculation. This improves mathematical precision while leaving the principal convergence results and empirical evidence unchanged. Minor typesetting regressions in Appendix D slightly offset this focused gain.
